practice_items.atom_title: Wi-Fi basics and wireless security protocols (WPA2/WPA3)
practice_items.prompt: Which cipher suite does WPA2 use to provide both confidentiality and data integrity?
options: RC4-TKIP
AES-CCMP
DES-CBC
3DES-ECB
practice_items.explain: WPA2 uses AES in Counter Mode with CBC-MAC (CCMP), replacing the broken RC4-based WEP and TKIP.

practice_items.atom_title: Wi-Fi basics and wireless security protocols (WPA2/WPA3)
practice_items.prompt: What is the primary security advantage of WPA3-SAE over WPA2-PSK?
options: WPA3-SAE prevents offline dictionary attacks against captured handshakes
WPA3 uses a longer password by default
WPA3 does not require any password
WPA3 uses RC4, which is faster
practice_items.explain: SAE uses a zero-knowledge proof so captured handshake traffic cannot be used for offline brute-force or dictionary attacks.

practice_items.atom_title: Wi-Fi basics and wireless security protocols (WPA2/WPA3)
practice_items.prompt: A student says 'I hid my SSID so attackers cannot find my network.' What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Nothing is wrong; hidden SSIDs are invisible to all scanners
SSID hiding increases encryption strength
Hidden SSIDs still appear in probe responses and any passive scanner reveals them
SSID hiding is only available on WPA3
practice_items.explain: SSID hiding is security theater. Probe responses expose the network name to any passive wireless scanner in seconds.

practice_items.atom_title: Wi-Fi basics and wireless security protocols (WPA2/WPA3)
practice_items.prompt: Select ALL configuration choices that represent best practice for a school Wi-Fi network.
options: Use WPA2-AES or WPA3 for the student SSID
Use WEP for legacy device compatibility
Isolate guest devices on a separate VLAN
Keep AP firmware updated to patch protocol vulnerabilities
practice_items.explain: WPA2-AES/WPA3, VLAN isolation, and firmware updates are best practice. WEP is completely broken and must not be used.

practice_items.atom_title: Wi-Fi basics and wireless security protocols (WPA2/WPA3)
practice_items.prompt: Which WPA2 mode requires individual credentials via a RADIUS server and is preferred for corporate environments?
options: WPA2-PSK (Personal)
WPA2-OWE
WPA2-TKIP
WPA2-EAP (Enterprise)
practice_items.explain: WPA2-Enterprise uses 802.1X and a RADIUS server so each user or device has individual credentials and accountability.

practice_items.atom_title: Wi-Fi basics and wireless security protocols (WPA2/WPA3)
practice_items.prompt: Name the WPA3 property that ensures compromising today's session key cannot decrypt previously captured sessions.
practice_items.explain: Forward secrecy ensures each session derives fresh keys; past captured sessions remain protected even if the current key is exposed.

practice_items.prompt: What distinguishes a managerial (administrative) control from a technical control?
options: Managerial controls are policies/procedures enforced through training and process, not automatically by hardware or software
Managerial controls are always more expensive
Managerial controls only apply to physical security
There is no meaningful difference
practice_items.explain: Managerial controls are documented policies and processes governing human behavior, backed by training and review, rather than something enforced automatically by a technical mechanism.

practice_items.prompt: An organization requires new employees to sign a document defining permitted and prohibited use of company systems. What is this document called?
options: Firewall configuration
Acceptable Use Policy (AUP)
Access control list
Badge access log
practice_items.explain: An Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) defines what employees are and are not permitted to do with organizational systems and data.

practice_items.prompt: Which of the following are examples of managerial controls? Select ALL that apply.
options: A documented least-privilege access review process
A locked server room door
Annual security awareness training
A firewall rule blocking a malicious IP
practice_items.explain: A documented access-review process and awareness training are both policy/process-driven managerial controls. The locked door is a physical control, and the firewall rule is a technical control.

practice_items.prompt: Why is 'privilege creep' a problem that a least-privilege policy specifically addresses?
options: It refers to accounts gradually accumulating unnecessary access rights over time without review
It refers to passwords getting weaker over time
It only affects physical badge access, not digital accounts
It is a technical vulnerability in firewalls
practice_items.explain: Privilege creep happens when access rights accumulate as employees change roles without being revoked; a documented least-privilege review policy catches and corrects this over time.

practice_items.prompt: Name the recurring managerial control that teaches employees to recognize social engineering and follow security policy, often including simulated phishing emails.
practice_items.explain: Security awareness training is a recurring program (often annual, with phishing simulations) that changes employee behavior through education and reinforcement.

practice_items.prompt: A badge reader that requires a PIN and physical badge to open a data center door, is this a technical or physical control?
options: Physical, it restricts physical access to a space, regardless of using electronic components
Technical, anything involving electronics is automatically technical
Managerial, it requires an employee to remember a PIN
None of the above
practice_items.explain: Classification depends on what the control restricts (physical access to a space), not on whether it involves electronic components, this is a physical control.

practice_items.prompt: What is the core justification for defense in depth (layered defense)?
options: It is required by law in every jurisdiction
It reduces the total number of controls an organization needs
Every individual control has weaknesses or can be misconfigured, so no single control should be relied on alone
It guarantees an attacker can never succeed
practice_items.explain: Because every control has known or undiscovered weaknesses, or can be misconfigured, defense in depth ensures a single failure does not cause a full compromise.

practice_items.prompt: Endpoint antivirus/EDR software installed on individual employee laptops belongs to which defense-in-depth layer?
options: Perimeter
Human
Data
Host
practice_items.explain: Host-layer controls protect the individual device itself, assuming outer layers (perimeter, network) may fail.

practice_items.prompt: Which of the following are examples of network-layer controls (as distinct from perimeter or host)? Select ALL that apply.
options: VLAN segmentation separating departments
WPA3 wireless security protocol
A border firewall at the internet gateway
Full-disk encryption on a laptop
practice_items.explain: VLAN segmentation and WPA3 both operate inside the internal network to limit lateral movement and secure the wireless segment. The border firewall is perimeter-layer, and full-disk encryption is data-layer.

practice_items.prompt: Why does the human/managerial layer 'span' all the other layers rather than sitting at one specific point?
options: It only applies to physical security
It only matters during an active breach
It replaces the need for any technical controls
It keeps every technical layer correctly configured, monitored, and improved, and catches what automated controls miss
practice_items.explain: Policy, training, and process (the human/managerial layer) reinforce and maintain every technical layer, and often catch things automated tools miss, such as an employee reporting a phishing email.

practice_items.prompt: Name the layer that protects data itself (e.g., via encryption) regardless of which device or network segment it is currently on.
practice_items.explain: The data layer is the innermost layer, even if every outer layer fails, strong data-layer controls like encryption can still prevent stolen data from being usable.

practice_items.prompt: An organization deploys only a single, very strong perimeter firewall and no other controls. What is the main risk of this approach?
options: None, a strong enough single control is always sufficient
Firewalls are technically incapable of stopping any attacks
Different attack vectors (e.g., ARP spoofing on the internal network, phishing) bypass the perimeter entirely, so a single control leaves other layers completely undefended
It costs more than layered defenses
practice_items.explain: A single control, however strong, only addresses the attack vectors it specifically covers; other vectors (internal MITM, social engineering, compromised devices) require controls at other layers entirely.
